newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-Basque guerrilla became monk to help sufferers.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Basque guerrilla became monk to help sufferers.

text.p: A former member of one of ETA's bloodiest Basque guerrilla groups told a French court on Tuesday that he had become a monk and worked as a hospital priest to relieve sufferers.
Philippe Saez, 38, is on trial with five other suspected members of ETA's notorious "roving French commando", a squad held responsible for 37 killings in 1978-1989.
Some of the attacks targeted top army generals and shook the then young Spanish democracy.
Saez admitted he helped in attacks, but said he never killed. He left ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) in 1979 to join a monastery.
"I always had a yearning for the absolute. As time went by I told myself: 'I will join a monastery and no longer speak about my past," he said. "But the past came back."
Saez was detained when the French commando was smashed in 1990. He was transferred to house arrest in a Paris monastery a year later and afterwards allowed to become a hospital priest.
"I wanted to help those who suffer," he said.

At the psychiatric department of Paris' La Pitie-Salpetriere hospital, Saez met victims of bomb attacks on Paris commuter trains in 1995-96 blamed on Algerian Moslem fundamentalists and said he was moved by their "deep suffering".
Saez said he got interested in ETA during trips to Spain to study the traditional Basque flute, the txistu.
ETA has killed some 800 people in its three-decades-old campaign for a Basque state independent from Madrid.
Three of the co-defendants, Jean Parot, Jacques Esnal and Frederic Haramboure, left the courtoom on Tuesday saying the trial was unfair.

Defence lawyers have asked the court to summon as a witness Spain's detained former Civil Guard chief Luis Roldan. Judicial sources said Spain rejected the request. Roldan is in jail accused of corruption.
The commando is held responsible for killing senior Spanish army and navy officers, policemen, two magistrates, a businessman who refused to pay ETA "revolutionary taxes" and several passers-by.
In its bloodiest attack, it bombed a Civil Guard barracks in Saragossa in 1987, killing 12 people, including six children, and wounding 78.
The trial is expected to last until the end of the month.
